title: Battle of Waterloo
intro: On Sunday 18 June 1815 Napoleon's Armée du Nord met the Duke of Wellington's multinational army on the open farmland south of Waterloo, some fifteen kilometres from Brussels. Two days earlier Napoleon had beaten the Prussians at Ligny while Marshal Ney fought Wellington at Quatre Bras. On the 17th both allied armies fell back north, the Prussians to Wavre rather than east toward home, so they stayed within a day's march of each other. Wellington took up a low ridge at Mont-Saint-Jean astride the Brussels road, garrisoned three farms in front of it and kept most of his troops out of sight behind its crest, trusting Blücher's promise to march across from Wavre and join him. Napoleon, with Marshal Grouchy and a third of the army away chasing the Prussians, had to break Wellington before they came. The day became a race between the French assaults on the ridge and the slow Prussian march across the Lasne valley.
outcome: A decisive Coalition victory: the repulse of the Imperial Guard and the Prussian capture of Plancenoit broke the French army, and Napoleon abdicated four days later.
uncertainty: Witnesses' watches disagreed: the first attack on Hougoumont is timed anywhere from 10:00 to 11:30, and La Haye Sainte fell between 18:00 and 18:30; this map uses the times most modern accounts give. Strengths and losses vary by source. The Grand Battery's exact position is debated; it is drawn on a spur in front of d'Erlon's corps. Which Guard battalions attacked at 19:30, and in squares or columns, is still argued; this follows the five Middle Guard battalions in squares. Farms are placed at today's buildings; Rossomme, Smohain and the 1815 Bois de Paris are approximate, and the Lion's Mound later cut away the ridge west of the crossroads. Each block stands for many battalions, squares or batteries.

steps.title: Blücher marches to join Wellington
steps.narrative: Rain fell all night and the clay fields were still sodden at dawn. Wellington had said he would stand at Mont-Saint-Jean only if the Prussians sent him at least one corps; early on the 18th Blücher replied that he would come with three. Bülow's IV Corps, the one corps not mauled at Ligny, led the march from Wavre, but its columns and 88 guns crawled through the town's narrow streets, around a fire that blocked several of them, and along mud tracks; its rear only got clear around 10:00. Zieten's I Corps and Pirch's II Corps were to follow. Thirteen kilometres to the west, the two armies spent the morning forming up on facing ridges about 1,300 metres apart.

notes.text: Fire in Wavre delays Bülow's march
Wellington's army on the Mont-Saint-Jean ridge
Napoleon's army forms around La Belle Alliance

steps.title: Two ridges and three farms
steps.narrative: Wellington's line ran for about four kilometres along the Mont-Saint-Jean ridge, with the sunken Ohain road following its crest. As in Spain, he kept most of his infantry lying down just behind it, so the French could see only skirmishers and guns. Three groups of farm buildings in front of the ridge served as breakwaters: the walled château of Hougoumont on the right, La Haye Sainte beside the Brussels road in the centre, and Papelotte with the hamlets of Smohain on the left, where the Prussians were expected. Napoleon, unable to see the allied army, drew up symmetrically on the La Belle Alliance ridge: Reille's II Corps west of the road, d'Erlon's I Corps east of it, Kellermann's and Milhaud's cuirassiers behind them, and Lobau's VI Corps and the Imperial Guard in reserve. He let the ground dry before committing his guns and horses.

notes.text: Infantry lies hidden behind the crest
400 KGL riflemen hold La Haye Sainte

steps.title: The attack on Hougoumont
steps.narrative: The battle opened on the French left, where Jérôme Bonaparte's division pushed into the Hougoumont wood. Bauduin's brigade cleared the trees but was cut down by British guns on the ridge, and Bauduin was killed. Soye's brigade reached the walls, and a party led by Sous-Lieutenant Legros axed open the north gate, until Lieutenant-Colonel Macdonell and a few Guardsmen forced it shut; the Frenchmen trapped inside were killed. Napoleon hoped the attack would draw in Wellington's reserves, but it did the opposite: brigade after brigade of Reille's corps, eventually some 14,000 men, was fed into the fight for a farm that the Coldstream and 3rd Guards, steadily reinforced down the hollow lane behind it, held until nightfall.

notes.text: North gate forced, then shut again

steps.title: The Grand Battery opens; Prussians sighted
steps.narrative: Around midday some eighty French guns, massed on a spur in front of d'Erlon's corps, opened on the allied left centre. They could see little beyond the skirmishers and Bylandt's Dutch-Belgian brigade, and many balls buried themselves in the mud, but the bombardment still bled the battalions waiting behind the crest. At about 13:15 Napoleon made out dark columns near Chapelle-Saint-Lambert, six or seven kilometres to his right: Bülow's vanguard. He sent word for Grouchy to come west, turned Lobau's VI Corps and the light cavalry of Domon and Subervie to face the Bois de Paris, and moved his own post up to La Belle Alliance. Bülow halted at Chapelle-Saint-Lambert until his long column closed up before tackling the deep Lasne valley.

steps.title: D'Erlon's grand attack
steps.narrative: D'Erlon then sent about 14,000 infantry up the slope east of the road. His divisions advanced in echelon as enormous columns, each a block of eight or nine battalions stacked one behind another with a front of some two hundred men, hard to manoeuvre and slow to deploy. Quiot's division on the left split to surround La Haye Sainte, whose garrison held its walls. The columns drove in the skirmishers and reached the hedges of the sunken lane, where Bylandt's brigade gave way; Kempt's and Pack's brigades rose to fire, Picton was shot dead leading them forward, and for a few minutes the French were breaking into Wellington's left centre.

steps.title: The charge of the heavy cavalry
steps.narrative: Uxbridge, the allied cavalry commander, sent his two British heavy brigades over the crest. Somerset's Household Brigade, charging astride the road, swept away the cuirassiers screening the French flank and rode into the leading infantry; Ponsonby's Union Brigade burst through its own infantry and caught d'Erlon's columns while they were still struggling through the hedges. Packed too deep to form square, the French divisions collapsed: the Royals and the Scots Greys each took an eagle, and about 3,000 men were lost, over two thousand as prisoners. Only Durutte's division on the right kept its order. But the troopers would not rally, and on blown horses they galloped on across the valley into the Grand Battery, sabring its gunners.

steps.title: Cuirassiers and lancers strike back
steps.narrative: Napoleon answered at once. Two of Milhaud's cuirassier brigades and Jacquinot's lancers fell on the scattered British horsemen in the valley. Ponsonby was caught by lancers and killed, the Scots Greys were all but destroyed, and the two brigades suffered losses they never made good before the survivors regained their own lines, covered by Vandeleur's light dragoons and the Dutch-Belgian cavalry. The Grand Battery was soon firing again, but d'Erlon's corps needed until about 16:00 to re-form, and its attack had used up Napoleon's best chance of breaking the allied left before the Prussians arrived.

steps.title: Ney's cavalry against the squares
steps.narrative: Ney, commanding the front line, took the wounded streaming to the rear of Wellington's centre for the start of a retreat. With little infantry left to hand, he sent Milhaud's cuirassiers and the Guard light cavalry up the open slope between Hougoumont and La Haye Sainte, then added Kellermann's corps and the Guard heavy cavalry: around 9,000 horsemen in wave after wave. The allied infantry formed squares in a chequerboard behind the crest; the gunners fired until the last moment, sheltered inside, and returned to their pieces as each wave ebbed. No square broke. Wellington fed the Brunswickers into the line, pushed Adam's brigade forward above Hougoumont and called Chassé's division in from Braine-l'Alleud. Without infantry or guns close behind them, the charges used up the French cavalry instead.

notes.text: Allied infantry in squares; no square breaks

steps.title: Bülow strikes at Plancenoit
steps.narrative: While the horsemen fought on the ridge, Bülow's corps finished crossing the Lasne valley and came out of the Bois de Paris around 16:30, aiming at Plancenoit and the French rear. One brigade drove Lobau's men back from Frichermont while Hiller's brigade stormed Plancenoit, a village behind Napoleon's line and close to his only road of retreat. Napoleon sent the eight battalions of the Young Guard, who won the village back after savage fighting and then lost it again; two battalions of the Old Guard finally cleared it with the bayonet. Every man held at Plancenoit was a man Napoleon could not send against Wellington. Meanwhile Zieten's I Corps had set out from Wavre toward Ohain.

notes.text: Bülow emerges from the Bois de Paris, 16:30

steps.title: La Haye Sainte falls
steps.narrative: Ordered once more to take La Haye Sainte, Ney sent in rallied men of d'Erlon's corps led by the 13e Léger, with engineers and guns. The German riflemen had fired off nearly all their ammunition and the farm fell; only a few dozen got back to the ridge. Ney pushed horse artillery and skirmishers up to the farm and the knoll beside it and raked the squares at close range, and Ompteda's battalion, sent down to retake the farm, was ridden over by cuirassiers. West of it, Bachelu's and part of Foy's infantry tried a late combined attack and were shot back by Adam's brigade. Wellington's centre was perilously thin, but Zieten's van was appearing near Ohain, freeing Vivian's and Vandeleur's light cavalry to ride across behind the line to the centre.

notes.text: KGL out of ammunition: farm lost

steps.title: The Imperial Guard attacks
steps.narrative: With Plancenoit held for the moment, Napoleon committed his last reserve: five battalions of the Middle Guard in battalion squares, guns between them, with Old Guard battalions behind. Ney led them up the slope obliquely toward the allied right centre, while d'Erlon's rallied men pressed again east of the road. The grenadiers on the right drove back Colin Halkett's battered brigade until Chassé's fresh Dutch-Belgian division brought a horse battery onto their flank and charged with the bayonet. Further west the chasseurs topped the crest into point-blank volleys from Maitland's Foot Guards, who had been lying down out of the guns' sight. As the last chasseur battalion came on, Colborne swung the 52nd Light Infantry out of line onto its left flank and broke it. At Papelotte, Zieten's leading brigade, steered back to Wellington's flank by the liaison officer Müffling after a moment's hesitation, was coming into action against Durutte.

steps.title: The Guard falls back; the general advance
steps.narrative: The cry that the Guard was falling back ran along the French line, and with Zieten's Prussians breaking in near Papelotte, panic spread from the right. Wellington rode to the crest, raised his hat and sent the whole allied line forward, with Vivian's and Vandeleur's fresh light cavalry ahead of it. Guard battalions rallied in squares south of La Haye Sainte to cover the retreat, but Adam's brigade and the hussars swept them back toward La Belle Alliance. At Plancenoit the Prussians attacked for the third time while Pirch's II Corps worked round through the Chantelet wood to the south; the Guard defenders gave way, and the village changed hands for the last time. Reille's, d'Erlon's and Lobau's corps dissolved into crowds streaming south down the Charleroi road.

notes.text: Plancenoit falls for the last time

steps.title: Rout and pursuit
steps.narrative: Two Old Guard battalions in square beside La Belle Alliance were the last French formations on the field. Napoleon sheltered in one until his staff persuaded him to go, and both squares drew off in fair order into the dusk while everything else broke. Around 21:00 Wellington and Blücher met near the inn. The exhausted allied army halted on the field, and the Prussian cavalry under Gneisenau took up the pursuit by moonlight, driving the fugitives through Genappe, where Napoleon's carriage was captured. The French left almost all their guns behind and lost some 25,000 killed and wounded and thousands of prisoners, against about 17,000 allied and 7,000 Prussian casualties. Napoleon abdicated four days later.
